hero.title: Run agents that can’t
hero.lede: A self-hosted agent harness where the model holds no credentials and gets no shell. It proposes; a separate broker process authorizes, bounds it, and writes down what happened. Pre-production.

why.title: The model is the untrusted part.
why.intro: A harness hands a model instructions, tools, and a loop. Dekopon puts a separate authority layer around the tools.

cards.title: Anything the model reads can steer it.
cards.body: Messages, issues, tool results — anything the model reads can carry instructions someone else wrote. Dekopon treats whatever comes out the other side as a request, not an order.

cards.title: A real shell hands over the machine.
cards.body: Host files, inherited environment, open sockets — one bad line and the blast radius is the whole machine. Dekopon’s shell has none of them.

cards.title: Permission lives outside the prompt.
cards.body: Identity, policy, and credentials all live in a different process. No string, however persuasive, claims to be Alice or adds a host to the allowlist.

why.bridge: A blast radius you can read off a file before anything runs. Whatever the model gets talked into, it can only do what you granted by name — and no second model gets a vote.

journey.title: Alice may comment. Merge stays absent.
journey.intro: A synthetic PR-commenter agent, traced from the Slack message to the GitHub comment.

steps.label: Identify
steps.title: Slack authenticates Alice.
steps.body: The gateway carries a canonical Slack subject across the process boundary. The message can’t name its own principal.

steps.label: Propose
steps.title: The model asks to comment.
steps.body: Its one sandboxed tool turns a familiar gh command into a single narrow capability request.

steps.label: Decide
steps.title: The broker checks every boundary.
steps.body: Cedar decides whether Alice may take this action through this agent. Separate constraints pin the host, the methods, and the ceilings.

steps.label: Execute
steps.title: One fresh provider call runs.
steps.body: A fresh Wasm store gets only the host interfaces it was approved for. The broker’s own HTTP engine adds the token after checking the guest’s headers.

steps.label: Record
steps.title: The decision and the result stay linked.
steps.body: A hash-linked audit record ties the identity, the Cedar decision, and the outcome together. Prompt and response bodies are never stored.
steps.detail: invocation ID + trace ID + policy digest

journey.denied: Still denied: approve, merge, the rest of the GitHub API

security.title: Every control here has a limit.
security.intro: Dekopon doesn’t detect prompt injection or make a model trustworthy. It shrinks what a successful injection can reach.

rows.threat: Prompt injection or a model mistake
rows.control: The model can only propose capabilities that exist by name. The broker authorizes each call from trusted context it built itself.
rows.limit: Nothing here detects prompt injection. And on a persistent route, injected text sticks around for a while.

rows.control: Provider credentials never reach the prompt, the shell, or the Wasm guest. The broker’s own HTTP engine injects a destination-bound value.
rows.limit: Allowlist a host that echoes headers back and the token walks out. Pick your hosts.

rows.control: No OS bash, no inherited environment, no host files. Hosts, methods, and byte ceilings are all fixed before the agent starts.
rows.limit: If something hostile is already running as your user, you’ve lost. This doesn’t help you there.

rows.control: Identity comes from the authenticated transport and a mapping you wrote. Never from message text.
rows.limit: The local dev subject is caller-supplied. It’s off unless you turn it on, and nothing external vouches for it.

rows.control: Authorization is a Cedar policy file and owner-authored YAML, evaluated by native Rust. No model reviews, scores, or approves another model’s action.
rows.limit: Static rules can’t read intent. Grant a capability and it’s granted — the broker won’t notice that this particular comment was a bad idea.

rows.control: The Cedar decision, the outcome, and the trace ID all carry the same invocation ID.
rows.limit: The audit chain is local and unsigned. Anyone with your disk can rewrite it, and nothing here un-posts a comment.

limits: One local Unix UID is currently one trust domain
No independent audit anchor, no incident-response automation

useCases.title: Five providers, five separate repos.
useCases.intro: Each one is a Wasm component with a fixed list of operations. None of them hands the model a general API.

items.label: GitHub
items.title: Comment, approve, and merge are three separate grants.

items.title: Read Wikipedia without a fetch tool.

items.label: Ripgrep
items.title: Real ripgrep, zero host imports.
items.body: Real Rust regex matching over documents you hand it. The paths are labels — the provider never opens a filesystem.

items.label: Python
items.title: Python that can’t reach anything.
items.body: A fresh RustPython interpreter runs one bounded script. No files, no network, no subprocesses.

items.label: SQL
items.title: Turso inside Wasm, storage outside it.
items.body: Turso reaches two logical durable files through one exact storage import. The guest never gets a host path.

broker.title: Every limit lives in one YAML file.
broker.intro: The story above, as the file you actually write. Alice, one operation, one destination — all fixed before the agent starts.
broker.yaml:
apiVersion: dekopon.dev/brokerd/v1alpha1
brokerPrincipal: local-broker
policyRevision: pr-commenter-2026-08
policiesPath: ./policies.cedar
credentialsPath: ./broker-credentials.yaml
providers:
  - ./gh-provider.wasm

identities:
  - uid: 65532
    principal: chat-gateway
    actor: { type: service, principal: chat-gateway }
    attestor:
      namespaces: [slack.example]
      chatScopes:
        - breadth: transportWide
          kind: slack
          transport: workspace-slack
identityMappings:
  - subject: slack.example.u123
    principal: alice

constraintSets:
  gh.pull-request.comment:
    provider: gh
    effect: external-write
    risk: Medium
    idempotency: conditional
    credential: github-comment-token
    constraints:
      timeoutMs: 15000
      maxOutputBytes: 8192
      http:
        allowedHosts: [api.github.com]
        allowedMethods: [GET, POST]
        maxRequests: 2
        maxRequestBytes: 16384
        maxResponseBytes: 262144
        allowPlaintextLoopback: false

authority.title: Two Cedar rules,
authority.intro: Slack subject slack.example.u123 maps to principal alice. Two permit rules let her drive pr-commenter and ask it for one GitHub comment.
authority.decisionBody: The rule matches trusted identity and routing context. It never reads Alice’s message or the provider input.
authority.constraintsTitle: The broker then applies the YAML envelope
authority.denial: Route Alice to release-bot and Cedar denies agent.prompt before any model call: the Agent resource no longer matches.

invariants.title: Text can’t become Alice
invariants.body: The principal comes from gateway attestation and a mapping you wrote. Never from the prompt.

invariants.title: Driving the agent isn’t using it
invariants.body: Permission to prompt pr-commenter doesn’t include permission to use its GitHub capability.

invariants.title: Comment isn’t merge
invariants.body: Every capability is its own Cedar action, and a missing one is a denied one.

invariants.title: Policy can’t widen I/O
invariants.body: Cedar decides whether the action happens. It can’t add a host, a method, or a byte to what happens next.

execution.title: A shell with no operating system underneath.
execution.intro: Models already write bash fluently — pipes, loops, exit codes. Dekopon keeps that habit inside a language with no processes, no files, and no sockets.
execution.script:
set -euo pipefail
issue=$(tickets issue show T-42)
echo "$issue" | jq '{title, owner, state}'

for id in $(tickets issue list --state open | jq -r '.[].id'); do
  tickets issue show "$id" | jq '{id, owner, state}'
done
execution.result: one script · bounded JSON · explicit exit codes

cards.title: Models already know this
cards.body: Variables, pipes, exit codes. It reads like the shell transcripts these models were trained on.

cards.title: Providers become verbs
cards.body: A provider may declare a command word. Its pure resolver turns argv into one typed capability proposal.

cards.title: A command grants nothing
cards.body: Resolving tickets issue show doesn’t authorize it. The same Cedar decision and the same broker limits still run.

cards.title: Every loop has a ceiling
cards.body: Script steps, model turns, provider fuel — everything has a number attached to it before the run starts.
